# Reflexes and Safety Enforcement\chaptersubtitle{System 1 1000 Hz Control Barrier Functions, Compliance, and Motor FOC}

![**Systems Organ Focus:** Stage 6 (Real-Time Reflex & 1 kHz Bare-Metal Safety Enforcers) across the Proposal–Permission Privilege Boundary. Dedicated bare-metal microcontroller silicon executes in zero-allocation static SRAM (`malloc=0`), solving Control Barrier Function Quadratic Programs (CBF-QPs) in $<175\,\mu\text{s}$ to minimally project candidate neural actions onto safe half-spaces before commanding $20\text{ kHz}$ Field-Oriented Control inverters.](figures/fig_pipeline_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch09 width=100% fig-pos="H"}

*Why does a software safety guardrail written in Python fail to stop a robot from injuring a human during an OS memory compaction pause?*

In cloud software systems, safety guardrails are implemented as application-level middleware filters, assertion checks, or wrapper scripts. In Physical AI, software safety checks co-located on a general-purpose operating system share the same execution thread, memory bus, and scheduling vulnerability as the neural models they are meant to supervise. When the host OS suffers a memory compaction stall, thread preemption, or runtime crash, unmanaged motor registers remain latched and moving mass crashes into the environment. Physical AI solves this structural failure through the Proposal–Permission Privilege Split: high-capacity neural models propose actions from an untrusted Linux domain, while a dedicated, bare-metal microcontroller executing in zero-allocation static SRAM holds exclusive electrical authority to evaluate Control Barrier Functions and veto hazardous commands in sub-millisecond real time.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-objective}
After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

1. **Implement Zero-Allocation 1000 Hz MCU Enforcers:** Construct hard real-time safety filters on dedicated ARM Cortex-M7 / lockstep RISC-V microcontroller silicon with bounded worst-case execution latency ($\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$) and zero dynamic heap allocation (`malloc=0`).
2. **Formulate Control Barrier Functions (CBFs):** Derive continuously differentiable barrier certificates $h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0$ guaranteeing the forward invariance of safe operating sets $\mathcal{C}$ under non-linear control-affine dynamics.
3. **Solve Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Programs (CBF-QPs):** Project unverified candidate action proposals ($\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$) emitted by neural policies onto admissible safety half-spaces ($\mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}$) using closed-form KKT active-set solvers in static SRAM.
4. **Enforce Dynamic Stopping Envelopes ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clearance}}$):** Intercept and veto trajectory proposals that violate clearance margins relative to stationary and moving obstacles before physical contact occurs.
5. **Implement Contact Impedance and Passivity Control:** Formulate virtual spring-damper compliance ($\mathbf{M}_d, \mathbf{D}_d, \mathbf{K}_d$) and passivity energy tanks to stabilize physical contact interactions.
6. **Command Motor Field-Oriented Control (FOC):** Direct $20\text{ kHz}$ Space-Vector Pulse-Width Modulation (SVPWM) switching via Clarke and Park transforms in dedicated hardware timer peripherals.
7. **Dissect OS Latency Blowout Collisions:** Analyze the Late Commanded Deceleration autopsy where a $140\text{ ms}$ Linux dirty page writeback stall caused a $3.4\text{ kN}$ collision that fractured a harmonic drive flexspline.
8. **Freeze the Safety Enforcement Interface:** Author the formal engineering specification (**SAFE-01**) establishing 1000 Hz timer schedules, CBF parameters, the IEC 60204-1 emergency stop hierarchy, and asynchronous re-anchoring handshakes.

**Core Chapter Takeaway:** Physical safety cannot be delegated to application software or learned neural policies; it requires a dedicated bare-metal System 1 permission authority operating at $1000\text{ Hz}$ in zero-allocation static SRAM (`malloc=0`) that solves Control Barrier Function Quadratic Programs (CBF-QPs) to minimally perturb candidate actions and guarantee forward invariance.
:::


## The Proposal–Permission Split: Why System 1 Holds Sole Hardware Authority

In conventional robotics software stacks, motion planning, trajectory optimization, and safety monitoring are frequently bundled into a monolithic application process executing under a standard operating system. In modern Physical AI architectures, where high-level reasoning and trajectory synthesis are powered by multi-billion parameter foundation models and diffusion decoders, this monolithic design is lethal.

A general-purpose operating system (such as standard Linux) is designed to optimize average throughput across competing processes. In doing so, it routinely introduces non-deterministic latency spikes: kernel memory compaction pauses, dirty page background flushes, thread preemption, and bus contention across shared DRAM crossbars (@fig-enforcer-timing). If safety monitoring resides in user-space software on the Linux host, any OS stall halts the safety monitor simultaneously with the neural policy. During that stall, moving mass continues to coast forward under unguided momentum ($d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t$), converting software latency directly into mechanical impact.

![**System 1 Microsecond Timer Waterfall and Proposal-Permission Boundary.** Dedicated bare-metal MCU executes a strict $1000\text{ Hz}$ ($1.0\text{ ms} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$) timer interrupt. Ingesting candidate spline waypoints from shared SRAM mailboxes, reading $1000\text{ Hz}$ joint telemetry, solving the Minimal-Intervention CBF-QP in $<175\,\mu\text{s}$, and writing Space-Vector PWM registers to drive motor inverters.](figures/fig08_enforcer_timing_waterfall.svg){#fig-enforcer-timing width=100%}

Physical AI resolves this fundamental vulnerability through the **Proposal–Permission Privilege Split**. The system is partitioned across heterogeneous silicon into two strictly isolated operational domains:

1. **The Untrusted Proposal Domain (System 2 & System 1.5):** Large Vision-Language Models (VLAs) and generative trajectory decoders (ACT, Diffusion Policies) execute on multi-core Linux Application Processors (MPUs) and edge Neural Processing Units (NPUs). This domain possesses rich semantic intelligence and wide receptive fields but is treated from a safety standpoint as an **Untrusted Proposal Service**. It generates candidate trajectory chunks and expiring intent leases, depositing them into lock-free shared memory mailboxes.
2. **The Sole Hardware Permission Authority (System 1):** A dedicated, hard real-time microcontroller (e.g., ARM Cortex-M7 or dual-core lockstep RISC-V) executes bare-metal or on a microsecond RTOS kernel in tightly coupled static SRAM. This microcontroller possesses **exclusive physical routing** to the gate drivers of the motor inverters. It evaluates candidate trajectory chunks against non-negotiable physical invariants at a deterministic $1000\text{ Hz}$ ($1.0\text{ ms} \pm 5\,\mu\text{s}$) cadence.

The microcontroller firmware strictly obeys the **Iron Law of Deterministic Execution (`malloc = 0`)**: zero dynamic heap allocations, zero blocking mutexes, and zero reliance on operating system threads. Every matrix, buffer, and data structure is allocated statically at compile time. By bounding the worst-case execution time to $\text{WCET} \le 175\,\mu\text{s}$, the System 1 enforcer guarantees that safety invariants are evaluated with microsecond precision, ensuring the physical survival of the machine even if the host Linux operating system crashes or freezes.


## Control Barrier Functions (CBFs): Forward Invariance and Admissible Safe Sets

In empirical machine learning, researchers frequently attempt to enforce safety by adding penalty terms to a reward function during reinforcement learning or by adding loss penalties during behavioral cloning. On physical hardware, soft loss penalties are fundamentally inadequate: they merely alter statistical probability distributions, readily permitting catastrophic constraint violations when the system encounters novel out-of-distribution inputs.

Physical safety requires a hard, mathematically provable guarantee of **Forward Invariance** [@ames2014control; @ames2019control]. Consider a continuous non-linear control-affine dynamical system:

$$\dot{\mathbf{x}} = f(\mathbf{x}) + g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u}$$

where $\mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \subset \mathbb{R}^n$ represents the physical state vector (joint positions, velocities, and obstacle distances) and $\mathbf{u} \in \mathcal{U} \subset \mathbb{R}^m$ represents the commanded actuator control input (motor torques or phase voltages).

We define the admissible **Safe Operating Set** $\mathcal{C} \subset \mathcal{X}$ as the super-level set of a continuously differentiable scalar function $h: \mathcal{X} \to \mathbb{R}$:

$$\mathcal{C} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \;\middle|\; h(\mathbf{x}) \ge 0 \right\}$$

$$\partial \mathcal{C} = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \;\middle|\; h(\mathbf{x}) = 0 \right\} \quad (\text{Safe Boundary})$$

$$\text{Int}(\mathcal{C}) = \left\{ \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{X} \;\middle|\; h(\mathbf{x}) > 0 \right\} \quad (\text{Interior Safe Region})$$

The safe set $\mathcal{C}$ is **Forward Invariant** if for every initial state starting within the set ($\mathbf{x}(0) \in \mathcal{C}$), the trajectory remains strictly inside the set for all future time ($\mathbf{x}(t) \in \mathcal{C}, \forall t \ge 0$).

By **Nagumo's Theorem**, forward set invariance is guaranteed if the time-derivative of the barrier certificate $\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u})$ is bounded from below by an extended class-$\mathcal{K}$ function $\alpha(h)$:

$$\dot{h}(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{u}) = \frac{\partial h}{\partial \mathbf{x}} \dot{\mathbf{x}} = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot f(\mathbf{x}) + \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) \cdot g(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} \ge -\alpha(h(\mathbf{x}))$$

Utilizing the standard Lie derivative notation ($L_f h(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) f(\mathbf{x})$ and $L_g h(\mathbf{x}) = \nabla h(\mathbf{x}) g(\mathbf{x})$), the fundamental **Control Barrier Function (CBF) Condition** is expressed as:

$$L_f h(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} + \alpha(h(\mathbf{x})) \ge 0$$

where $\alpha(h) = \gamma h$ ($\gamma > 0$) specifies the rate at which the system is permitted to approach the safety boundary. When the system is far inside the safe interior ($h(\mathbf{x}) \gg 0$), $-\alpha(h)$ is a large negative number, imposing virtually zero constraint on candidate control inputs. However, as the state approaches the boundary ($\mathbf{x} \to \partial \mathcal{C} \implies h(\mathbf{x}) \to 0$), $-\alpha(h) \to 0$, forcing the system's velocity toward the boundary to decelerate to zero, rendering the safe set mathematically impenetrable.


## Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Programming (CBF-QP): Active-Set Solvers in Microsecond SRAM

To merge unverified candidate action proposals from generative neural models ($\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$) with hard physical safety guarantees, the System 1 microcontroller solves a **Minimal-Intervention Control Barrier Function Quadratic Program (CBF-QP)** at every $1000\text{ Hz}$ control cycle (@fig-cbf-projection).

![**Minimal-Intervention Quadratic Programming Projection.** The unverified candidate action $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$ generated by the neural policy is projected onto the admissible half-space $\mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}$ defined by active Control Barrier Function hyperplanes. When the proposal is safe, it passes unmodified ($\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$); when it threatens a barrier breach, the QP minimally alters the command to ensure forward invariance.](figures/fig08_cbf_projection.svg){#fig-cbf-projection width=100%}

The optimization problem is formulated as:

$$\mathbf{u}^* = \arg\min_{\mathbf{u} \in \mathbb{R}^m} \frac{1}{2} \left\| \mathbf{u} - \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} \right\|_{\mathbf{W}}^2$$

$$\begin{aligned}
\text{subject to} \quad &L_f h_i(\mathbf{x}) + L_g h_i(\mathbf{x})\mathbf{u} + \alpha_i(h_i(\mathbf{x})) \ge 0, \quad i = 1, \dots, M_{\text{barriers}} \\
&\mathbf{u}_{\text{min}} \le \mathbf{u} \le \mathbf{u}_{\text{max}} \quad (\text{Actuator Current / Torque Limits})
\end{aligned}$$

where $\mathbf{W} \succ 0$ is a diagonal weighting matrix penalizing control effort.

The mathematical beauty of the Minimal-Intervention QP resides in the **Minimal Perturbation Principle**:
1. **Unconstrained Execution:** As long as the neural policy's candidate proposal $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$ satisfies all barrier constraints ($L_f h_i + L_g h_i \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}} + \alpha(h_i) \ge 0$), the unconstrained optimum is achieved, and the solver outputs the exact neural command unmodified: $\mathbf{u}^* = \mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$.
2. **Active-Set Projection:** When a candidate action threatens to breach a barrier (e.g., commanding an arm toward an obstacle or exceeding joint velocity limits), the barrier constraint becomes active. The quadratic program computes the orthogonal projection of $\mathbf{u}_{\text{cand}}$ onto the boundary of the admissible half-space $\mathcal{U}_{\text{safe}}$, altering the control input only by the exact mathematical minimum necessary to preserve safety.

Because this optimization must complete in $<175\,\mu\text{s}$ inside an embedded microcontroller, the solver utilizes closed-form active-set methods (such as embedded qpOASES or OSQP) operating entirely on pre-allocated static SRAM arrays with zero dynamic memory allocation.


## Real-Time Dynamic Stopping Envelopes and Clearance Monitoring ($d_{\text{stop}} \le d_{\text{clearance}}$)

At every millisecond tick, the System 1 microcontroller monitors the physical clearance separating the machine from environmental obstacles. In physical reality, a moving mass cannot be arrested instantaneously: arresting kinetic energy requires finite mechanical distance and time.

The total **Dynamic Stopping Distance** $d_{\text{stop}}(v)$ is derived by summing the reaction displacement consumed during sensorimotor transport latency and the physical braking distance required under maximum deceleration:

$$d_{\text{stop}}(v) = \underbrace{v \cdot \tau_{\text{latency}}}_{\text{Reaction Drift}} + \underbrace{\frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}}}_{\text{Kinematic Braking}}$$

where $v = \|\dot{\mathbf{x}}\|$ is the Euclidean operational velocity, $\tau_{\text{latency}}$ is the total worst-case hardware latency (including sensor exposure, communication, and inverter filter delays, typically $12.0\text{ ms}$), and $a_{\text{max}}$ is the certified maximum emergency braking deceleration.

The fundamental safety invariant evaluated at $1000\text{ Hz}$ requires that the available physical clearance $d_{\text{clearance}}(\mathbf{x})$ must strictly exceed the dynamic stopping distance plus a safety margin $d_{\text{margin}}$:

$$d_{\text{clearance}}(\mathbf{x}) \ge d_{\text{stop}}(v) + d_{\text{margin}} = v \cdot \tau_{\text{latency}} + \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}} + d_{\text{margin}}$$

If a high-level trajectory proposal attempts to command an approach velocity that violates this inequality, the System 1 enforcer overrides the candidate setpoint, commanding a dynamic deceleration clamp that matches the approach velocity to the available clearance envelope.


## Contact Impedance Control: Virtual Spring-Damper Dynamics and Passivity Enforcement

While rigid position control is effective for free-space motion, it is hazardous during physical contact manipulation. When a robotic manipulator interacts with a rigid surface (such as inserting a peg, polishing a workpiece, or contacting a human operator), minor geometric calibration errors generate extreme contact force spikes:

$$F_{\text{contact}} = k_{\text{env}} \cdot \Delta x$$

Because the stiffness of steel or aluminum fixtures exceeds $k_{\text{env}} > 10^6\text{ N/m}$, a positional tracking error of just $0.5\text{ mm}$ produces contact forces exceeding $500\text{ N}$, stalling motors and destroying precision gear teeth.

To achieve safe physical interaction, Physical AI replaces rigid position setpoints with **Joint and Cartesian Impedance Control** [@hogan1985impedance]. Rather than enforcing a rigid coordinate, the microcontroller regulates the dynamic relationship between external interaction forces $\mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}$ and kinematic displacements, rendering the end-effector as a programmable virtual mass-spring-damper system:

$$\mathbf{M}_d (\ddot{\mathbf{x}} - \ddot{\mathbf{x}}_d) + \mathbf{D}_d (\dot{\mathbf{x}} - \dot{\mathbf{x}}_d) + \mathbf{K}_d (\mathbf{x} - \mathbf{x}_d) = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}$$

where $\mathbf{M}_d, \mathbf{D}_d, \mathbf{K}_d \succ 0$ are the desired virtual inertia, damping, and stiffness matrices, and $\mathbf{x}_d(t)$ is the nominal reference trajectory from the candidate chunk.

The commanded motor joint torques $\boldsymbol{\tau}^*$ are computed at $1000\text{ Hz}$ using the manipulator Jacobian $\mathbf{J}(\mathbf{q})$ and gravitational compensation $\mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})$:

$$\boldsymbol{\tau}^* = \mathbf{J}^T(\mathbf{q}) \left[ \mathbf{K}_d (\mathbf{x}_d - \mathbf{x}) + \mathbf{D}_d (\dot{\mathbf{x}}_d - \dot{\mathbf{x}}) \right] + \mathbf{g}(\mathbf{q})$$

To guarantee that variable impedance gains never inject non-physical energy that could destabilize contact, the microcontroller implements **Passivity Observers and Energy Tanks** [@ferraguti2013energy], monitoring instantaneous energy exchange ($P(t) = \mathbf{F}_{\text{ext}}^T \dot{\mathbf{x}}$) and scaling damping injection to guarantee that the closed-loop system remains strictly passive ($\int_0^t P(\tau) d\tau \ge -E_{\text{tank}}(0)$).


## Motor Field-Oriented Control (FOC): Space-Vector PWM and Stator Flux Alignment

At the physical boundary where digital control setpoints become analog electromagnetic forces, the microcontroller commands brushless permanent magnet synchronous motors (PMSMs) using **Field-Oriented Control (FOC)** executing at $20\text{ kHz}$ in hardware timer peripherals.

FOC decouples the three-phase AC stator currents ($i_a, i_b, i_c$) into two orthogonal DC current components rotating synchronously with the rotor magnetic flux:

1. **Clarke Transformation:** Maps 3-phase currents onto a 2-phase stationary orthogonal reference frame ($\alpha, \beta$):

$$\begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 & 0 \\ 0 & \frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} & -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}} \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_a \\ i_b \\ i_c \end{bmatrix}$$

2. **Park Transformation:** Projects stationary currents onto the rotating rotor reference frame ($d, q$) using the optical joint encoder angle $\theta_e$:

$$\begin{bmatrix} i_d \\ i_q \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta_e & \sin\theta_e \\ -\sin\theta_e & \cos\theta_e \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} i_\alpha \\ i_\beta \end{bmatrix}$$

The **Direct Axis Current ($i_d$)** controls the rotor magnetic flux alignment (regulated to $i_d = 0$ for non-salient motors to maximize efficiency), while the **Quadrature Axis Current ($i_q$)** produces electromagnetic torque in direct proportion to the torque constant $K_t$:

$$\tau_{\text{motor}} = \frac{3}{2} P \cdot \lambda_{\text{pm}} \cdot i_q = K_t \cdot i_q$$

where $P$ is the number of motor pole pairs and $\lambda_{\text{pm}}$ is the permanent magnet flux linkage.

The resulting voltage setpoints $(v_d^*, v_q^*)$ are transformed back into three-phase pulse-width modulation duty cycles using **Space-Vector PWM (SVPWM)**, driving the gate voltages of isolated MOSFET/IGBT H-bridge inverters at $20\text{ kHz}$.

To protect motor windings from thermal destruction during sustained high-torque operations, the firmware executes a real-time **$I^2t$ Thermal Accumulator**:

$$E_{\text{thermal}}(t) = \int_0^t I_{\text{phase}}^2(\tau) R_{\text{stator}} d\tau$$

When stator temperature exceeds the warning knee ($T_{\text{stator}} > 85^\circ\text{C}$), the microcontroller initiates linear torque derating, preventing insulation breakdown at $155^\circ\text{C}$.


## Systems Failure Anatomy: The Late Commanded Deceleration & Operating System Latency Tails

The fatal consequences of hosting safety checks in user-space software on a general-purpose operating system are documented in the forensic autopsy of a 6-DoF industrial articulated manipulator.

::: {.callout-autopsy title="The Late Commanded Deceleration"}
**Platform:** 6-DoF Articulated Material-Handling Manipulator ($v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$).  
**Failure Mechanism:** Host Linux application processor experienced a $140\text{ ms}$ dirty page writeback memory compaction pause while approaching an obstacle at $d_{\text{clearance}} = 0.280\text{ m}$.  
**Root Cause:** Arm coasted unguided for $0.252\text{ m}$ during the OS pause; when software resumed, remaining clearance was only $0.028\text{ m}$ ($2.8\text{ cm}$), rendering safe braking ($d_{\text{brake}} = 0.081\text{ m}$) physically impossible.  
**Physical Consequence:** Wrist struck a steel fixture plate at $0.92\text{ m/s}$ ($3.4\text{ kN}$ dynamic impact), catastrophically fracturing the Joint 4 harmonic drive flexspline ($7,200\text{ USD}$ overhaul).  
:::

![A 6-DoF articulated manipulator arm in the testbed, highlighting the specific harmonic drive wrist joint that fractured during the collision incident.](figures/fig08_manipulator_arm_cropped.jpg){#fig-enforcement-platform width=100%}

In this industrial workcell incident, the 6-DoF articulated manipulator was executing high-speed palletizing maneuvers at $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$ (@fig-enforcement-platform). Safety monitoring and trajectory generation were co-located in a user-space Python/C++ node executing under a standard Linux distribution on an x86-64 host computer.

At timestamp $T - 0.140\text{ s}$, an optical time-of-flight range sensor detected an unexpected fixture protrusion at a distance of $d_{\text{clearance}} = 0.280\text{ m}$. However, at that exact millisecond, the Linux kernel initiated a background memory compaction cycle to service a multi-gigabyte dirty page writeback. The user-space planning and safety process was preempted and suspended for $140\text{ ms}$.

Because the motor inverters were governed by unmanaged user-space setpoints, the actuators held the last commanded velocity. The arm coasted forward unguided:

$$d_{\text{coast}} = v \cdot \Delta t_{\text{pause}} = 1.8\text{ m/s} \times 0.140\text{ s} = 0.252\text{ m}$$

When the Linux kernel finally resumed the safety process at $T - 0.010\text{ s}$, the remaining physical clearance had collapsed to:

$$d_{\text{remaining}} = 0.280\text{ m} - 0.252\text{ m} = 0.028\text{ m} = 2.8\text{ cm}$$

The safety software immediately commanded maximum emergency braking deceleration ($a_{\text{max}} = 20.0\text{ m/s}^2$). However, the quadratic braking distance required to arrest moving mass from $v = 1.8\text{ m/s}$ was:

$$d_{\text{brake}} = \frac{v^2}{2 a_{\text{max}}} = \frac{1.8^2}{2 \times 20.0} = \frac{3.24}{40.0} = 0.081\text{ m} = 8.1\text{ cm}$$

Because the required stopping distance ($8.1\text{ cm}$) exceeded the remaining physical clearance ($2.8\text{ cm}$), the collision was physically unavoidable. The manipulator struck the solid steel fixture plate at an impact velocity of $v_{\text{impact}} \approx 0.92\text{ m/s}$, generating a dynamic shock load of $F_{\text{impact}} \approx 3.4\text{ kN}$. The shock load fractured the precision flexspline teeth of the Joint 4 harmonic drive speed reducer, bent the mounting flange, and destroyed internal motor bearings ($7,200\text{ USD}$ overhaul cost). The flight-recorder telemetry ledger is detailed in @tbl-telemetry-ch09.

| **CBF Invariants** | `geofence_box`<br>`min_clear_m`<br>`max_force_n`<br>`cbf_gamma` | $[[-0.35, 0.35], [0.10, 0.60], [0.00, 0.50]]\text{ m}$<br>$0.015\text{ m}$ ($15\text{ mm}$ floor)<br>$12.5\text{ N}$ continuous interaction force<br>$\gamma = 15.0\text{ s}^{-1}$ (Class-$\mathcal{K}$ convergence) |

## Master Capstone Synthesis of Part II

With the completion of the real-time safety enforcement layer, we conclude Part II's systematic journey through the **Five Cognitive Organs of Physical AI**. 

Across Chapters 5 through 9, we have constructed the complete, closed-loop cyber-physical pipeline from first principles:

$$W_t \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 5}]{\text{Perceive}} O_t \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 6}]{\text{Remember}} S_t \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 7}]{\text{Reason}} I_t (\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}) \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 8}]{\text{Plan}} \tau_t (p_t) \xrightarrow[\text{Ch 9}]{\text{Execute}} u_t^* \xrightarrow{\text{Actuation}} W_{t+1}$$

1. **Perception (Chapter 5):** Transduced raw photon fluxes into compact 3D metric affordance tokens in $SE(3)$ using zero-copy DMA pipelines and self-supervised ViT spatial encoders.
2. **Memory (Chapter 6):** Sustained continuous spatial belief across visual occlusions through Lie algebra coordinate frame trees, JEPAs, and expanding uncertainty envelopes.
